pKa of the –COOH group: 2.3. pKa of the –NH₃⁺ group: 9.6.

buffer-properties-s3.title: The buffer in blood
buffer-properties-s3.html: Blood plasma is buffered mainly by carbonic acid and hydrogen carbonate: H₂CO₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + HCO₃⁻(aq), with pKa = 6.1 at body temperature. Normal blood has pH 7.4 and contains about 20 times as much HCO₃⁻ as H₂CO₃.

items.q: Acetic acid is titrated with NaOH; the equivalence point is at pH 8.72. Which indicator is the best choice?
Ammonia is titrated with HCl; the equivalence point is at pH 5.28. Which indicator is the best choice?
What color is bromothymol blue in a solution at pH 9.5?
In a solution at pH 5.4, what is the ratio [In⁻]/[HIn] for bromocresol green?

mistakes.why: Value: that is [HIn]/[In⁻]. pH is above pKa, so the deprotonated form In⁻ is in the majority and the ratio is above 1.

items.q: A 0.0010 M strong acid is titrated with 0.0010 M strong base. Because the solutions are so dilute, the steep rise near equivalence (pH 7.00) runs only from about pH 6 to 8. Which indicators would give an accurate end point? Select all that apply.
Which box is at pH 7.0?
options: The volume of each box is needed to tell

items.q: Box 1 is brought to pH 3.0 by adding a strong acid. How does the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] change?
At pH 5.0, what percentage of the acid is in the A⁻ form?

mistakes.why: Value: a ratio of 1 : 10 means 1 part A⁻ in 11 parts total, not 1 in 10. Percent = 1/(1 + 10) × 100.

items.q: A medicine is absorbed through cell membranes only in its uncharged form, HA (pKa 6.0). In which region would it be absorbed best?
options: Blood and the stomach equally, at pH 7.4 and 2

items.q: Which form of glycine predominates at pH 7?
Which form of glycine predominates at pH 11?
At pH 3.00, what is the ratio [–COO⁻]/[–COOH] for glycine's carboxylic acid group? (Take its pKa as 2.30.)

mistakes.why: Value: pH is above pKa, so the deprotonated form is in the majority: 10^(pH − pKa) = 10^(+0.70), above 1.

items.q: A glycine solution at pH 7 is made more basic, to pH 10.5. Predict the change in each.

variables.name: Fraction of amine groups that are –NH₃⁺
Fraction of acid groups that are –COO⁻

items.q: A weak acid has pKa 4.2. In a solution at pH 2.2, which form predominates?
options: HA and A⁻ in equal amounts

items.q: Put these steps for choosing an indicator in order.
options: Decide what is in the flask at the equivalence point
Estimate the equivalence-point pH (7, above 7 or below 7)
Find an indicator whose pKa is close to that pH
Check that its range (pKa ± 1) falls on the steep part of the curve

items.q: A student titrates acetic acid with NaOH using methyl orange (pKa 3.5) as the indicator. How will the measured volume of NaOH compare with the true equivalence volume?
options: Smaller, because the color changes early in the buffer region
Larger, because the color changes after the equivalence point
Equal, because any indicator marks the equivalence point
Larger, because methyl orange reacts with some of the NaOH

items.q: Methylammonium, CH₃NH₃⁺, has pKa 10.64. What fraction of methylamine is in the protonated form at pH 9.64? Give your answer as a decimal.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the deprotonated fraction. pH is below pKa, so the protonated form CH₃NH₃⁺ is in the majority.
Value: one pH unit below pKa is a 10 : 1 ratio, not 100 : 1. Fraction = 10/(10 + 1).

items.q: A student says, "At pH 7 every weak acid is mostly deprotonated, because 7 is neutral." Which acid shows the claim is wrong?
Which claim do the data support?
options: The acetic acid / acetate mixture resists a pH change
The three solutions resist a change in pH to the same extent
NaCl solution is a buffer because it contains ions
Water resists a change in pH better than the mixture

items.q: Which equation shows how the mixture removes the added acid?
options: H₃O⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O + H₂O (with OH⁻ from water)

items.q: Show how the "pH after" for the mixture was calculated: find the pH after the HCl is added.

mistakes.why: Value: the changes run the wrong way. Added H₃O⁺ uses up acetate (0.010 → 0.009 mol) and makes acetic acid (0.010 → 0.011 mol).
Value: that ignores the buffer. The H₃O⁺ reacts with acetate first.

items.q: After the HCl is added to the buffer, predict the change in each compared with before.
Two OH⁻ ions are added to Box 1. Which box shows the result?
A student adds two H₃O⁺ ions to Box 1 and draws Box 4 as the result. What is wrong with the drawing?
options: The H₃O⁺ should have reacted with A⁻, giving 7 HA and 3 A⁻
The H₃O⁺ should have reacted with HA, giving 3 HA and 7 A⁻
Nothing is wrong: added ions stay free in a buffer
The H₃O⁺ should have become two OH⁻ ions

items.q: The weak acid has pKa 4.74. What is the pH of the solution shown in Box 2?

mistakes.why: Value: the ratio is inverted. [H₃O⁺] = Ka × [HA]/[A⁻] = Ka × 7/3.

items.q: Box 1 is diluted with water to twice its volume. How does its pH change?
options: It stays about the same, because the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] is unchanged
It rises by about 0.30, because the concentrations are halved
It falls, because water is added
It rises to 7, because the buffer is diluted

items.q: During hard exercise, lactic acid enters the blood. Which reaction keeps the pH from dropping sharply?
Taking pKa = 6.10, what is [HCO₃⁻]/[H₂CO₃] in blood at pH 7.35, the low end of the normal range?

mistakes.why: Value: that is [H₂CO₃]/[HCO₃⁻]. pH is above pKa, so the base form is in the majority.

items.q: Based on its 20 : 1 ratio, the blood buffer is better at neutralizing which kind of addition?
options: Added acid, because there is much more HCO₃⁻ than H₂CO₃
Added base, because there is much more HCO₃⁻ than H₂CO₃
Both equally, because it is a buffer
Neither, because pH 7.4 is far from pKa

items.q: A person hyperventilates (breathes fast), removing CO₂, which lowers [H₂CO₃] in the blood. Predict the change in each.
Two buffers are made with the same weak acid: Buffer A has 0.10 M HA and 0.10 M A⁻; Buffer B has 1.0 M HA and 1.0 M A⁻. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: Buffer B can absorb more added acid before its pH changes much
Buffer B has a lower pH, because it has more acid
Buffer A has a higher pH, because it is more dilute

items.q: Why does a buffer contain a weak acid and its conjugate base, rather than a strong acid and its conjugate base?
options: The conjugate base of a weak acid is a strong enough base to react with added H₃O⁺
Strong acids have no conjugate base
Weak acids make H₃O⁺ faster than strong acids

items.q: A 1.00 L buffer contains 0.250 mol CH₃COOH and 0.250 mol CH₃COONa (pKa 4.74). What is the pH after 0.050 mol of NaOH is added (no volume change)?

mistakes.why: Value: added OH⁻ converts HA to A⁻, so the acid goes down (0.200 mol) and the conjugate base goes up (0.300 mol).
Value: that treats the NaOH as if no buffer were present. It reacts with the acetic acid first.

items.q: A student writes: "A buffer keeps its pH constant no matter what is added." Which correction is best?
options: A buffer limits the change; the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] still shifts a little
A buffer keeps its pH constant for added base but not for acid
A buffer works by changing its Ka to match whatever is added
A buffer keeps its pH constant until it is heated

items.q: A student needs a buffer at pH 7.40. Which acid and conjugate base pair is the best choice?
What is the pH of a buffer that is 0.25 M HCOOH and 0.15 M HCOONa?

mistakes.why: Value: the ratio is upside down. pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]): base on top.
Value: you used ln instead of log in the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation. It is the base-10 log.

items.q: What is the pH of a buffer that is 0.30 M NH₃ and 0.20 M NH₄Cl?

mistakes.why: Value: you used pKb of NH₃ (4.74). The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation needs pKa of the acid of the pair, NH₄⁺: 9.25.
Value: the base, NH₃, goes on top of the ratio: log([NH₃]/[NH₄⁺]).

items.q: For an acetic acid / sodium acetate buffer at pH 5.00, what ratio [CH₃COO⁻]/[CH₃COOH] is needed?

mistakes.why: Value: that is [CH₃COOH]/[CH₃COO⁻]. pH 5.00 is above pKa, so the base must be in the majority.
Value: you undid an ln instead of a log. The ratio is 10^(pH − pKa).

items.q: How many grams of NH₄Cl (53.49 g/mol) must be dissolved in 0.500 L of 0.200 M NH₃ to make a buffer at pH 9.00? Include the unit.

mistakes.why: Value: the ratio is inverted. pH 9.00 is below pKa 9.25, so NH₄⁺ must outnumber NH₃: mol NH₄⁺ = mol NH₃ / 10^(pH − pKa).
Value: you used pKb (4.74) in place of pKa of NH₄⁺ (9.25).

items.q: How many mL of 0.100 M NaOH should be added? Include the unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that gives a 1 : 1 ratio, pH 4.74. For pH 5.04 the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] must be 10^0.30 = 2.0, so more base is needed.
Value: x mol OH⁻ makes x mol A⁻ and leaves (0.0100 − x) mol HA, so solve x/(0.0100 − x) = 2.0, not x = 2.0 × 0.0100.

items.q: Diluting the mixture to 250.0 mL in the volumetric flask changes which quantity?
options: Both concentrations, but not the pH
The pH, because the acid becomes more dilute in the flask
The ratio [A⁻]/[HA], because water is a base
The pKa, because the volume changes

items.q: Which step would best confirm that the buffer was made correctly?
options: Measure its pH with a calibrated meter
Check that the final solution is clear and colorless
Weigh the volumetric flask before and after filling
Add phenolphthalein and check that it stays colorless

items.q: Put the steps of the buffer preparation in order.
options: Rinse a buret with 0.100 M NaOH, then fill it
Pipet 50.0 mL of 0.200 M acetic acid into a beaker
Add the calculated volume of NaOH from the buret and swirl
Transfer to a 250.0 mL volumetric flask, rinsing the beaker into it
Dilute to the mark with distilled water, stopper and invert to mix

items.q: Use the graph to find the pKa of HA.

mistakes.why: Value: read the pH where log([A⁻]/[HA]) = 0 (ratio 1), not where it equals 1.

items.q: What is the slope of the line, and what does it confirm?
options: 1, as predicted with a base-10 log
2.303, because the equation uses the natural log
−1, because more base lowers the pH
pKa, because the line passes through it

items.q: A student plots the same data with ln([A⁻]/[HA]) on the x-axis instead. What changes?
options: The slope falls to 0.434; the intercept stays
The slope becomes 2.303 and the intercept moves
Nothing changes, because ln and log are the same

items.q: Predict the pH of a buffer of this acid with [A⁻]/[HA] = 0.40.

mistakes.why: Value: you used ln. The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation uses the base-10 log: pH = 7.52 + log(0.40).
Value: the sign is reversed. log(0.40) is negative, so the pH is below pKa.

items.q: A buffer contains 0.0200 mol CH₃COOH and 0.0200 mol CH₃COO⁻ (pKa 4.74). What is the pH after 0.0050 mol HCl is added?

mistakes.why: Value: added acid uses up acetate and makes acetic acid; the base goes down to 0.0150 mol, the acid up to 0.0250 mol.
Value: you used ln instead of log.

items.q: A buffer has [A⁻]/[HA] = 1.0 × 10⁻². How far is its pH from pKa?
A student makes an ammonia buffer and calculates its pH as 4.92 using pH = pKb + log([NH₃]/[NH₄⁺]). What is the error?
options: It needs pKa of NH₄⁺, 14.00 − pKb
The equation should use ln for a base
Nothing: ammonia buffers are acidic solutions

items.q: Which expressions give the pH of a buffer of HA and A⁻? Select all that apply.
Which buffer has the largest capacity for both added strong acid and added strong base?
What is the pH of Buffer Q after 0.010 mol HCl is added?

mistakes.why: Value: added acid lowers the acetate (0.050 → 0.040 mol) and raises the acetic acid (0.050 → 0.060 mol).

items.q: Buffer R is much better at handling one kind of addition than the other. Which, and why?
options: Added base, because it has 0.90 mol CH₃COOH to react with OH⁻
Added acid, because its pH is below pKa
Added acid, because it has 0.90 mol CH₃COOH to react with H₃O⁺
Both equally, because a buffer resists acid and base the same

items.q: What is the pH of Buffer R after 0.15 mol HCl is added? (The buffer is overwhelmed: find the excess first.)

mistakes.why: Value: 0.10 mol of the HCl was taken up by acetate; only the excess, 0.05 mol, stays as H₃O⁺.

items.q: Which pairs of buffers have the same pH but different capacities? Select all that apply.
Which statement does the graph support?
options: Buffer 1 has the larger capacity: its pH stays nearly flat until about 0.10 mol NaOH
Buffer 2 has the larger capacity, because its pH rises sooner
The buffers have different pKa values, because they start at different pH
The capacities are equal, because both start at pH 4.74

items.q: The pH of each buffer rises sharply once its HA is used up. How many moles of HA did Buffer 2 contain at the start? (Read where its steep rise is centered.)

mistakes.why: Value: that is Buffer 1. Buffer 2's steep rise is centered near 0.020 mol NaOH.
Value: that is the total of HA and A⁻. OH⁻ reacts only with HA, so the steep rise comes when the HA (half the total) is used up.

items.q: How do the compositions of the two buffers most likely differ?
options: Buffer 1 has about five times the moles of both HA and A⁻
Buffer 1 has five times as much HA but the same A⁻
Buffer 1 uses a stronger weak acid

items.q: Buffer 1 is diluted with water from 1.00 L to 2.00 L before the NaOH additions. Predict the change in each.

variables.name: Moles of NaOH needed to use up the HA

items.q: Which two boxes have the same pH?
options: Each box has a different pH, because each holds a different number of particles

items.q: Three OH⁻ ions are added to each box. Which box can no longer act as a buffer afterward?
Two H₃O⁺ ions are added to Box Z. Which statement is correct?
options: Its A⁻ is used up, so Z stops being a buffer
Z resists well, because it has the most HA
Z is unchanged, because it has more acid than base

items.q: The acid has pKa 4.74. What is the pH of Box Z after three OH⁻ ions are added?

mistakes.why: Value: that is Box Z before the addition. Three OH⁻ convert three HA to A⁻: 7 HA and 5 A⁻.
Value: the ratio is inverted; base goes on top: log(5/7).

items.q: Rank these 1.00 L buffers of the same acid by their capacity for added strong base, smallest first.
A student wants a buffer at pH 7.0 with a large capacity for both acid and base. Which plan is best?
Why does a buffer work best within about one pH unit of its pKa?
options: Outside that range one component is less than a tenth of the other, so it is quickly used up
Outside that range the weak acid becomes strong
Outside that range water reacts with the buffer

items.q: Which salts become more soluble when the solution is made more acidic? Select all that apply.
Which explanation correctly says why adding HNO₃ dissolves more CaF₂(s)?
options: H₃O⁺ turns F⁻ into HF, so Q < Ksp
HNO₃ increases the Ksp of the CaF₂ solid
NO₃⁻ ions react with Ca²⁺ to form a soluble compound
The H₃O⁺ ions attack the solid and break its covalent bonds

items.q: How does adding HNO₃ change the solubility of AgCl?
options: Very little: Cl⁻ does not react with H₃O⁺
It increases, because H₃O⁺ reacts with Cl⁻ to form HCl
It decreases, because NO₃⁻ is a common ion
It increases, because salts dissolve better in acid

items.q: Of CaF₂ and BaCO₃, whose solubility rises more sharply as pH is lowered from 7 to 5, and why?
options: BaCO₃: CO₃²⁻ is the stronger base
CaF₂, because HF has the larger Ka
Both equally, because both anions are bases
CaF₂, because it releases two anions per formula unit

items.q: Which box best represents the solution after a strong acid is added to Box 1 and equilibrium is restored?
In every box, the total number of F atoms (in F⁻ and HF) should be twice the number of Ca²⁺ ions. Why?
options: Both come from CaF₂, with two F per Ca
Ca²⁺ has a 2+ charge, so it attracts two water molecules

items.q: A strong acid is added to the saturated CaF₂ solution with solid present. Predict the change in each once equilibrium is restored.
A student claims, "Adding acid dissolves CaF₂ because the acid raises Ksp." Which evidence from Boxes 1 and 2 contradicts the claim?
options: Box 2 contains more Ca²⁺ than Box 1

items.q: In which tube does the most Mg(OH)₂ dissolve?
Why does even less Mg(OH)₂ dissolve in Tube C than in Tube A?
options: OH⁻ is a common ion, so Q reaches Ksp sooner
NaOH reacts with Mg(OH)₂ to form a new solid

items.q: Put the steps of the explanation for Tube B in order.
options: H₃O⁺ reacts with OH⁻ to form water
The net dissolving reaction proceeds until Q = Ksp again, so more solid dissolves

items.q: A student repeats Tube B with 1.0 M NaCl instead of 1.0 M HCl. What result is expected?
options: About as little as in water: NaCl adds no H₃O⁺
As much dissolves as in HCl, because both contain Cl⁻
More dissolves than in HCl, because Na⁺ reacts with OH⁻
Nothing dissolves, because Cl⁻ is a common ion

items.q: Tooth enamel is mostly hydroxyapatite, Ca₅(PO₄)₃OH. Why do acidic drinks wear it away?
options: H₃O⁺ removes its OH⁻ and PO₄³⁻ ions
Acid raises the Ksp of hydroxyapatite
Acid adds Ca²⁺, a common ion, to the enamel
Acid makes the phosphate ions larger and looser

items.q: For which salts would adding NaOH (raising the pH) have little effect on solubility through acid-base reactions? Select all that apply.
Which claim about pH and solubility is correct?
options: A salt with a basic anion dissolves more at lower pH
Any salt dissolves more as pH decreases
A salt becomes more soluble as pH decreases because acid increases Ksp
A salt with a strong-acid anion becomes more soluble as pH increases
